en.title: Emily Wilson Tackles The Odyssey Again, Defying Publisher and Critics
en.summary: After a wildly successful translation and a public spat with Christopher Nolan's film adaptation, Emily Wilson is undertaking a complete retranslation of Homer's epic.
en.body:
The academic and translation world is abuzz as **Emily Wilson**, the acclaimed translator whose 2017 rendering of Homer's **The Odyssey** became a surprise bestseller and inspired **Christopher Nolan**'s film adaptation, has announced plans for a *complete* retranslation of the ancient epic. This isn't a minor revision; Wilson is starting from scratch, a decision she admits is "very controversial" with her publisher, but one she feels compelled to pursue.

Wilson’s previous translation achieved monumental success, selling over a million copies and earning praise for its accessibility and fresh perspective. However, the ensuing film adaptation by Nolan, which Wilson publicly panned in July, seems to have spurred her to revisit the text entirely. Her criticisms of the film were sharp, calling parts of the script "ashamed" and highlighting problematic character archetypes. While she later rescinded some specific points, her overall dissatisfaction with the cinematic interpretation appears to have fueled a desire to offer an even more definitive version of Homer’s masterpiece.

## A Translator's Bold Move

In the realm of classical translations, undertaking a full retranslation is exceptionally rare. Translators often issue revised editions to correct minor errors or refine their approach based on new scholarship or reader feedback. However, a complete overhaul signals a profound re-engagement with the text. Wilson's publisher, while perhaps initially hesitant due to the commercial risk, seems to have embraced her vision, with one editor noting that "her new approach is bound to be thrilling." This bold step underscores Wilson's commitment to capturing the nuances of **The Odyssey** in a way that resonates with contemporary readers, irrespective of previous interpretations or adaptations.

## The Discourse and Its Echoes

Wilson's critiques of Nolan's film, and her subsequent decision to retranslate, have ignited a lively debate. Literary figures and online commentators have weighed in, with some, like **Joyce Carol Oates**, questioning the timing and motivation of a translator who has benefited from the film's success. Yet, the sheer sales of Wilson's first translation suggest a massive audience eager for her insights. This renewed effort is not just an academic exercise; it’s a cultural event that speaks to the enduring power of ancient stories and the passionate fanbases they cultivate, proving that even millennia-old epics can generate compelling, modern discourse.

## What's Next

Details regarding the publication timeline for Emily Wilson's new translation of **The Odyssey** have not yet been announced. Readers eager for her latest take on the epic journey will need to stay tuned for further updates from her publisher.

content_raw: Undeterred and perhaps encouraged by the wave of conversation (and astronomical book sales) surrounding Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , Emily Wilson has announced plans to translate Homer’s epic yet again. Bucking the trend of announcing another AI-generated version of the movie, Wilson tells The Associated Press she’s embarking on a “complete retranslation” of the text, “not a revision of the old version.” Wilson’s previous translation, released in 2017, was a massive best-seller and received a shoutout from the Oscar-winning filmmaker as the inspiration for his adaptation. Nevertheless, Wilson panned the film in July , offering such generous criticisms as “I’d be ashamed to have written any part of this script” and accusing the actors of versions of the Black best friend, whose only role in the drama is to provide aid to the white protagonist.” She has since rescinded that last criticism and released a second takedown of the film , deragotorially comparing The Odyssey to Die Hard .  For those not keeping up with the Classics, while translators correcting and altering their work is common practice, a complete, ground-up retranslation is practically unheard of. So much so that Wilson says her decision was “very controversial” with her publisher. However, considering her first translation sold more than a million copies, we’re unsurprised that her editor believes “her new approach is bound to be thrilling.” Wilson’s film critiques weren’t without its critics. Smelling chum in the discourse, apex poster Joyce Carol Oates described the criticisms of “this person, who has benefited enormously from Nolan’s film” as beyond the pale: “One would expect a translator, of all people, beholden to a text, in service to a text, to be just a wee bit more thoughtful & respectful of others who are acting in good faith just as (she would claim) she is.” Wilson doesn’t fear controversy, particularly not from adults obsessed with children’s literature. Elsewhere in her interview with AP , she dared to call Percy Jackson “not designed for an adult literary reader” and describes the joys of becoming a publicly discussed academic. She adds, “The last few weeks have been a clear illustration of how I’m not in control of the reception of my work […] I actually think in some ways there’s a useful reminder about the powerlessness that comes with the awareness that ‘I’m going to be misunderstood. I’m going to be misread. People are going to hate me.’ I’ve got to accept that.” Judging by this video of her forceful recitation of the opening of The Odyssey in ancient Greek, we can assume Emily Wilson can take the heat.
